hook: the Chmielnicki uprising destroys Jewish communities in Ukraine
carry: a number that stands for real people

segments.voice: Yesterday, England: a door left unlocked, and Jews quietly readmitted. Your line was readmitted. A new week begins, and it begins far to the east, with a hard memory. Go gently today. Day nine hundred sixty.

Jewish memory has its own way of naming years. In the Hebrew calendar, years are written with letters, and two short letter-words, tach and tat, came to stand for a time of terror in Poland and Ukraine. Jews spoke of the decrees of tach and tat the way other people say a date they cannot forget. In the ordinary calendar, the first of those years is a single number. It is today's word.
screen: `YEARS WRITTEN IN LETTERS.` → `TACH AND TAT.` → `A NUMBER THAT IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: In the lands of Ukraine then ruled by Poland, the Cossacks rose up under a leader named Bohdan Chmielnicki. The uprising had its own grievances, against Polish lords and their power over the land and the people who worked it. Jews were caught in the middle. Some served the lords as stewards and leaseholders, collecting rents and running mills and inns, and so in the rebels' eyes they stood for the lords. As the rebel forces moved through towns, Jewish communities were attacked and destroyed. People fled to fortified towns, and some of those towns fell. Families were killed, taken captive, or forced to convert. The chronicles of the time give large numbers, and historians still argue over them. What no one disputes is that whole communities disappeared. A survivor named Nathan Hannover wrote a chronicle of those years. He gave it a title from the Psalms, from a cry of someone drowning: "I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no standing." In Hebrew, deep mire is yeven metzulah, and that became the book's name. He wrote it in plain Hebrew, so that people would know what had happened, town by town. Afterward, the rabbis of Poland set aside a day of fasting and lament, and some communities kept it long afterward. A massacre in these lessons is not a plot twist. It is a number that stands for real people, names mostly lost, held in a people's memory. That is what 1648 means here.
screen: `AN UPRISING AGAINST POLISH LORDS.` · `JEWS CAUGHT IN THE MIDDLE.` · `WHOLE COMMUNITIES DESTROYED.` · `DEEP MIRE, WHERE THERE IS NO STANDING.` · then, large: `1648.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember a massacre in silence. Sit still. Let your breathing slow, and let your hands rest open. You don't need to picture anything violent. Just hold in mind that there were towns, and in them families: someone baking bread, a child learning letters, an old man at prayer. Let the silence be for them. If thoughts come, let them pass. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words, or with no words at all. The bell holds the time.
Yeven metzulah. Deep mire, the name a survivor gave his chronicle of 1648, when Jewish communities in Ukraine were destroyed. Today's word.
Your line: a number that stands for real people. Today, when you see a date in the news tied to loss, pause for a breath before you scroll on. Day nine hundred sixty.
